content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an alternative way of formulating bilevel optimization problems into a NSgame for realizing the efficient learning. The main idea of NSgame is splitting the one variable in the classic Stackelberg game as two parts under the Nash game learning framework, where there are two competitive players who can achieve an equilibrium point. As a result, the new formulation can reduce the computational complexity of solving the original bilevel problem significantly. Also, it is shown in this work that the local Nash equilibrium point condition is sufficient to the strong differential Stackelberg equilibrium and a two time scale stochastic gradient descent method is proposed for obtainning this class of points. Multiple numerical results show that the proposed algorithm can have better performance than the classic meta learning ones, especially in terms of the computational complexities.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strength of this work is mainly about the proposed NSgame, including the connection between this model and the Stackelberg game, efficient algorithm design for solving this class of problems, and corresponding convergence analysis as well as multiple numerical verification of the theory.

The weaknesses of this paper are as follows:
1) although the studied problem is very interesting, only a very restrict class of problems is considered. From Def. 2.1 and 2.2., they basically imply that the considered problems are strongly convex (it needs the uniqueness of the global optimal point), which fails to cover a wide range of deep neural nets oriented machine/representation learning problems. Note that the existing works on Stackelberg game are provably to achieve statoinary points rather than only the gloal optimal one. So, even the computational issue can be reduced, but the scope of the applicability of this formulation is limited.

2) the obtained local Nash equilibrium of the NSgame is a SDSE point, which cannot find the differential Stackelberg equilibrium.

3) There is no convergence rate analysis provided, therefore, it is hard to say that whether the saved computational complexity can compensate the iteration complexity. Note that the existing bilevel optimization algorithms have been shown to achieve the global optimal solution for strongly convex problems.

4) it seems that the numerical results are based on the deep neural nets. Does this setting can satisfy the conditions given in the theory regarding the existence of the local Nash equilibrium or SDSE？
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: in general this paper is well written and it has presented the main contributions obtained in both theory and experiments.

Quality: the applicability of the studied model is limited. And assumption 3.1. is very strong, e.g., in the meta-learning setting, it needs the invariant space and adaptation part to be separable, which violates the motivation of performing meta-learning. Also, the convergence results are rather weak, as the iteration complexity is ignored completely. There is no clue whether this formulation can indeed save the total computational costs.

Novelty: to the best of my knowledge, this formulation is new and interesting, while proofs of the connection between the local Nash equilibrium point and SDSE as well as the convergence are truly straightforward, which just follow the standard proving techniques. Please let me know what the main challenges are.

Reproducibility: a limited number of source codes is attached in the appendix. It is hard to verify if they are reproducible or not. But from the description of the content, I believe that the results should be reproducible, especially since the report accuracy is not too high to believe.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, it is a very interesting topic and this work makes the connections between the NSgame and two other classic games. The major concerns lie in the quality and contributions of this work. A more sufficient analysis is needed based on the current stage of this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper studies the problem of bi-level optimization that has several applications in the machine learning community, including meta-learning based approaches to hyper-parameter optimization, robust training and training under class imbalance or noisy labels. 

Unfortunately, solving these bi-level optimization problems can be very slow especially when the nested optimization problem involves training deep neural networks. The key bottleneck is computing derivatives through the nested optimization problem which involves computing some second order derivative.

The authors observe that such a difficulty is not shared by Nash games where players play simultaneously instead of sequentially as in the bi-level problems which have a Stackelberg game structure.

The key focus of this work is to study when the original bi-level game can be decomposed into a combination of a small nested optimization problem and a bigger Nash equilibrium game. Specifically they propose a Nash game where the first player has a simple utility function and the other player's utility is expressed by a bi-level problem with a small nested problem. 

The paper provides both theoretical conditions on when this reduction works as well as experimental results in meta-learning applications showing that their optimization approach is faster while yielding comparable results with existing methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Regarding strengths, the paper proposes a novel approach to accelerating bi-level optimization, a notoriously slow problem to solve that has many applications of interest for the machine learning community. Indeed uncovering the structure of optimization problems to decompose them into several smaller is intuitive and could be very promising.

This work makes employs the following observations inspired by existing applications: 
i) the structure of bi-level problems for hyper-parameter optimization (e.g., Equation (17)). These motivate the notion of strong DSE. 
ii) the notion of coherence (Definition 3.2) that also applies to real life hyper-parameter optimization problems (see for example Theorem A.1). To the best of my knowledge the use of these observations to accelerate bi-level optimization is novel and unique to this work.

Unfortunately, the organization and the clarity of the work is a major weakness. Equation (3) is directly presented after some minimal preliminaries without providing any concrete intuition about why this approach was chosen. After trying to piece together the intuition throughout the paper and its appendix, I am still not sure how these decompositions of $y=(y_1,y_2)$ are actually chosen. Splitting the parameters of a neural network is mentioned as an example but it is not clear why/when this should work or which assumptions are critical. Instead every assumption is mentioned as mild, indicating that we get "an almost free lunch". It is not clear what stops us from just switching the Stackelberg game into a Nash game while still allowing a small Stackelberg game to work (see comments on experiments as well). 

I also have difficulties understanding the theoretical arguments of this work. For example, the connections to Pareto optimality of Equation (3)  are not very clear to me. Looking at the proof of Proposition 3.1 in the Appendix, the part about Pareto optimality is missing.

Regarding the experiments, it is unclear to me if in Figure 3 we could just choose $y_2$ to be the empty set. Would we expect it to work well? If so, wouldn't this imply that the nested problem formulation is not really useful in the first place?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: In my opinion, the clarity problems are significant. Although there are novel ideas as discussed above, it is hard for me to fully grasp how the decomposition of the problem actually works. Although there are a lot of reproducibility related details in the appendix, the experimental section has limited stand-alone value because most of the setup is deferred in the appendix.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, given the clarity issues I do not have a clear understanding of the work and I cannot recommend acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to alleviate the computational inefficiency in the bi-level optimization problem emerging from meta-learning or hyperparameter optimization. The main idea (NSGame) is to disentangle part of the follower $y$ from the Stackelberg game to a Nash game. Theoretical analysis is provided for the Differential Stackelberg Equilibrium (DSE), Differential Nash Equilibrium (DNE), and Strong DSE (SDSE). Experiments show NSGame can achieve performance comparable to previous methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The design is well-motivated. Indeed, the inner loop usually has massive parameters and cannot be solved efficiently. The idea of approximating the Stackelberg problem with the partial Nash problem is interesting.
2. Experiments on toy examples and real-world tasks show that this approximation is meaningful and can provide comparable results.

Weakness:
1. Most of the theoretical claims are not strong enough. The relations between DSE, SDSE, and DNE are relatively trivial given the assumptions. Some claims have problematic proof. Please see the next section for more details.
2. Assumption 3.1 seems too strong to hold for any real-world tasks. Especially, for the first term, it requires $f_1(x,y) = h(x) + \phi(y)$ to be separated into two independent functions. In scenarios like hyperparameter tuning, this is particularly untrue because that means minimizing the validation error is equivalent to fixing a set of optimal parameters for the network, and only tuning the hyperparameter.
3. The motivation of transform Eqn (1) to Eqn (3) is not really clear to me. I believe the authors' argument is that this transformation will reduce the inner loop's parameters. Then why not directly transform Eqn (1) to Eqn (2)? This is especially weird when the authors suggest $x$ represents hyperparameters, $y_1$ represents encoders like the ResNet and $y_2$ represents the top linear classifier. In this case, it seems only the top linear classifier participates in the bi-level hyperparameter tuning. I think the authors should add a discussion on why the formulation of Eqn (3) is more meaningful than both Eqn (1) and Eqn (2), both of which have mature solutions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Since the paper proposes a new methodology, I think it should spend more space explaining why this new methodology is better than others. To this end, this paper does not provide enough explanation.

2. For Proposition 3.1, my first impression is: the proof will apply to any optimum anyway, no matter whether SDSE exists. Do the authors concur that any optimum of Eqn (1) must be SDSE? I believe this proof is problematic in that, if the global optimum does not satisfy the SDSE condition, you cannot just make a descend step because that will violate the inner constraint.

3. Another claim I see as improper is that in the Contribution paragraph, the authors claim that they propose TTS-SGD to solve NSGame, which can find SDSE. I believe the correct claim will be that TTS-SGD can only find DSE. To obtain SDSE, Assumption 3.1 must hold. It is also questionable to say this paper `develops' TTS-SGD as it is a very standard two-time-scale stochastic approximation algorithm. Borkar indeed proved asymptotic convergence via ODE arguments. 

4. As mentioned in Weakness 3., shouldn't the ablation study also compare with pure Nash Equilibrium optimization? That is to make all parameters $y_1$. The computation cost, accuracy (Fig3), and gap of the loss (Fig 4) can help support the design of NSGame.
content.summary_of_the_review: The current state of this paper does not contain significant theoretical contributions and the experiments do not show a strong lead. Thus I recommend rejection.

content.title: DELVING INTO THE HIERARCHICAL STRUCTURE FOR EFFICIENT LARGE-SCALE BI-LEVEL LEARNING
content.abstract:
Recent years have witnessed growing interest and emerging successes of bi-level learning in a wide range of applications, such as meta learning and hyper-parameter optimization. While current bi-level learning approaches suffer from high memory and computation costs especially for large-scale deep learning scenarios, which is due to the hierarchical optimization therein. {\textit {It is therefore interesting to know whether the hierarchical structure can be untied for efficient learning}.} To answer this question, we introduce NSGame that, transforming the hierarchical bi-level learning problem into a parallel Nash game, incorporates the tastes of hierarchy by a very small scale Stackelberg game.
We prove that strong differential Stackelberg equilibrium (SDSE) of the bi-level learning problem corresponds to local Nash equilibrium of the NSGame. To obtain such SDSE from NSGame, we introduce a two-time scale stochastic gradient descent (TTS-SGD) method, and provide theoretical guarantee that local Nash equilibrium obtained by the TTS-SGD method is SDSE of the bi-level learning problem. We compare NSGame with representative bi-level learning models, such as MWN and MLC, experimental results on class imbalance learning and noisy label learning have verified that the proposed NSGame achieves comparable and even better results than the corresponding meta learning models, while NSGame is computationally more efficient.
